strengths: The manuscript presents an ambitious integration of multi-omic measurements, biomedical knowledge graphs, LLMs, and reinforcement-guided subgraph generation for CRISPR target prioritization. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/c1ebfeb6ac0d4b2a9b17b979cde96a04/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
Target-QA combines cell-line multi-omics, graph context, and CRISPR gene-effect labels, addressing a practically relevant biomedical task.
The main overall comparison includes several useful model families, and results are reported over multiple random seeds and many cancer-type subsets.
The generated subgraphs offer a potentially useful interface for inspecting model outputs, and the paper supplements them with pathway-enrichment case studies.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not convincingly establish generalization. Target-QA has only 363 cell lines and approximately 63 test instances, uses random splits, and contains highly correlated cell lines and broadly shared essential genes. Lineage-held-out, dependency-held-out, temporal, or external-dataset evaluation is absent, so the QA-tuned LLM may primarily learn common essential-gene frequencies. Calling the system patient-specific is also unsupported because all evaluations use cell lines.

The claimed contribution of graph process supervision is weakly isolated. Task-specific QA finetuning supplies nearly all of the improvement, while GALAX improves overall F1 only from 0.5094 to 0.5399 over L3-FT(QA). There are no controlled ablations of the immediate GNN reward, rollout reward, rule reward, graph-generator policy, pretrained graph encoder, or initial-node sources, and no significance tests are provided.

The reward model is poorly aligned with the stated objective. It is trained to distinguish cancerous from non-cancerous samples, whereas every Target-QA instance is cancerous and the downstream goal is cell-line-specific CRISPR target ranking. Maximizing generic cancer-class probability does not demonstrate that an intermediate edge is biologically correct or causally relevant to a predicted target.

The graph classifier itself is evaluated unreliably: it is trained on only 336 highly imbalanced samples, the best checkpoint is explicitly selected using test accuracy, and only accuracy/F1 are reported. An always-cancer predictor would already achieve about 88% accuracy on the stated 59-versus-8 test composition. This weakens the foundation of the process rewards.

Several evaluation quantities are unclear or internally problematic. Hit@5 is frequently higher than Hit@10, which is impossible for conventional hit-rate definitions; an appendix figure instead calls these precision@5 and precision@10. Metric definitions are missing, predicted-set sizes vary despite instructions to output exactly 100 genes, and some cancer-specific results are based on only one to seven test samples.

The biological validation is circular and insufficient. Disease annotations and curated biomedical interactions are used to retrieve candidates and construct rewards, after which enrichment against related curated resources is presented as independent evidence. No matched random-subgraph controls, held-out biological databases, external CRISPR screens, expert assessment, or experimental validation are included.

The central interpretability claim is not demonstrated. The paper shows that selected subgraphs contain recognizable pathways, but does not test faithfulness, stability across runs, edge validity rates, counterfactual effects on predictions, or agreement with known causal mechanisms. The policy can propose arbitrary node pairs and merely penalizes invalid relations, so structural validity is not guaranteed by the formulation.

Important methodological and reproducibility details remain ambiguous, including omics imputation for modalities with extensive missing samples, candidate ranking and tie handling, exact edge feasibility rules, reward normalization, optimal-subgraph selection, inference randomness, NER/API settings, and computational cost. The manuscript also contains inconsistent notation, dataset counts, terminology, and several strong claims of robustness, significance, and clinical grounding that are not supported by the experiments.

Novelty and positioning are incomplete. The work does not adequately compare against graph-explanation, rationale-extraction, RL-based subgraph-selection, or established gene-dependency prediction methods. Consequently, the experiments do not show that the proposed mechanism is preferable to simpler learned retrieval or graph-rationale approaches.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: integrating quantitative multi-omics, biomedical graphs, and language models for interpretable target prioritization.
The proposed pipeline combines language-model adaptation, graph representation learning, and sequential subgraph generation in a potentially interesting way.
The manuscript provides substantial implementation detail, several baseline variants, multiple randomized runs, cohort-level results, and qualitative pathway-enrichment examples.
weaknesses: The central reward is fundamentally misaligned with the claimed task. The GNN reward model is trained to distinguish cancerous from non-cancerous cell lines, yet it is used to judge whether partial subgraphs identify cell-line-specific CRISPR dependencies and biologically valid mechanisms. Maximizing a generic cancer-class probability does not establish target relevance, mechanistic correctness, or explanation faithfulness.

The evaluation does not rule out trivial prediction strategies. Each label contains 100 targets, many essential genes are shared across cell lines, and the paper omits essential baselines such as globally frequent targets, cancer-type frequency lists, nearest-neighbor retrieval, and direct supervised ranking from omics. The strong task-finetuning results could therefore largely reflect learning common target frequencies.

The random split of only 363 cell lines provides weak evidence of generalization. Samples from the same cancer types occur in training and testing, while prompts explicitly include cell-line and disease identities. There is no cancer-type-held-out, temporal, external-dataset, or patient-level evaluation, despite repeated claims of patient-specific and clinically grounded reasoning.

The reported ranking metrics are inadequately defined and internally suspicious. Hit@5 is consistently higher than Hit@10, which is impossible for the conventional cumulative Hit@K definition. The appendix instead labels these quantities precision@5 and precision@10. This inconsistency makes a major portion of the reported evidence uninterpretable.

The claimed improvements over the strongest task-tuned baseline are modest, no statistical significance tests are supplied, and uncertainty is reported across changing random splits without sufficient protocol detail. Statements that GALAX 'significantly' and consistently outperforms alternatives are consequently unsupported.

The ablations do not isolate the claimed innovations. There are no controlled removals of rollout rewards, the cancer-classification reward, rule rewards, greedy acceptance, biomedical initialization, or sequential construction, nor comparisons against random, shortest-path, or conventional learned subgraph selection.

The explanation evidence is circular and insufficient. Generation starts from disease-associated proteins and is constrained by a curated biomedical graph, after which enrichment against related curated pathway and disease databases is presented as validation. There are no matched random-subgraph controls, expert assessments, perturbation tests, ground-truth mechanisms, stability measurements, or faithfulness analyses.

The reward classifier is applied to small partial subgraphs despite being trained on full sample graphs, with no evidence that its probabilities remain calibrated or meaningful under this severe distribution shift. Its edge-prediction AUC of 0.644 also provides limited support for calling it an authoritative biological supervisor.

Model selection for the graph classifier explicitly uses test accuracy, contaminating that evaluation. Other methodological ambiguities and inconsistencies—including unclear candidate-edge constraints, dataset counts, metric extraction, baseline tuning, and the relationship between the four evaluation seeds and five finetuning trials—further weaken reproducibility.

The manuscript overstates clinical significance: all experiments use established cancer cell lines and retrospective DepMap labels, with no patient data, prospective CRISPR validation, drug-response validation, or comparison to experimentally supported novel targets. The evidence therefore does not support reliable precision-medicine or mechanism-discovery claims.

strengths: GALAX presents an interesting and relevant combination of LLM reasoning, graph neural networks, and reinforcement-guided subgraph construction for multi-omic target prioritization.
Using a pretrained graph classifier as a process-level reward model is a potentially useful way to obtain intermediate supervision without manually annotated reasoning traces.
The new Target-QA resource combines multi-omic measurements, biomedical graph knowledge, and CRISPR-derived targets, addressing an important precision-medicine problem.

The overall experiments include several meaningful comparison classes, including omics-only, GNN, language-model, static-KG, and G-Retriever variants. GALAX improves overall F1 from 0.5094 for the strongest QA-tuned non-graph baseline to 0.5399, with results reported across randomized runs.
The generated subgraphs provide a more inspectable intermediate representation than an unconstrained textual chain of thought, and the paper supplies multiple pathway-enrichment case studies.
The manuscript is ambitious, generally understandable, and provides substantial implementation and dataset detail in the appendix.
weaknesses: The strongest claims about mechanistic explainability are not adequately validated. The reward model predicts cancer versus non-cancer status, so high-reward subgraphs may capture generic cancer-associated signals rather than causal, cell-line-specific CRISPR vulnerabilities. Known-edge validity and post-hoc pathway enrichment do not establish faithfulness or causal relevance.

The experimental sample is small: Target-QA contains only 363 cell lines and 63 test examples. Many reported cancer-specific results are based on only one to a few test samples, making broad claims of robustness and generalizability premature. There is no external-dataset, temporal, or leave-cancer-type-out validation.

The paper reports no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals for comparisons. The overall improvement over QA-only finetuning is modest, and GALAX is not consistently best across individual cohorts or all ranking metrics, contrary to some of the manuscript's wording.

Model-selection practices raise concerns about optimistic bias. The graph model is explicitly selected using test accuracy, and the language-model sections describe choosing the best of five runs. It is unclear whether checkpoint/run selection ever uses the final evaluation set or how the four seeds underlying the reported results relate to these five runs.

The evaluation protocol and metrics need clearer definitions. In particular, Hit@5 is repeatedly higher than Hit@10, which is impossible for the conventional monotonic hit-rate definition. Precision and recall also differ despite both predictions and references nominally containing 100 targets, suggesting variable-length extraction or an undocumented computation.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed method's essential components. Missing studies include removal of the rollout reward, rule-based reward, graph-classifier reward, initial LLM candidates, graph pretraining, and greedy positive-reward filtering. Reward hacking, a central motivation, is neither measured nor stress-tested.

Several methodological details are ambiguous or inconsistent: the stated 80/20 split is actually 300/63, the relationships among pretraining, training, validation, and test cohorts are insufficiently audited for leakage, and the reward-weighted cross-entropy procedure is presented as reinforcement learning without comparison to standard policy-gradient alternatives.

The biological evaluation is largely post hoc and potentially circular because generated subgraphs are constrained by curated biomedical edges and then assessed for enrichment against related curated pathway databases. Expert annotation, perturbation-based validation, fidelity tests, or comparisons against established pathway-extraction methods would provide stronger evidence.

Reproducibility is weakened by blank code/data links in the submitted manuscript, dependence on GPT-4o-mini for entity extraction without sufficient versioning or stability analysis, and incomplete specification of some retrieval, decoding, and baseline-tuning procedures.

The clinical framing is stronger than warranted by experiments on established cancer cell lines. The work does not evaluate patient samples, prospective target discovery, treatment response, or laboratory confirmation, so claims of patient-specific and clinically grounded reasoning should be substantially qualified.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: integrating multi-omic measurements, biomedical knowledge graphs, and language models for cell-line-specific target prioritization.
GALAX is an ambitious, conceptually interesting pipeline combining an LLM, stepwise subgraph construction, a frozen GNN reward model, schema constraints, and rollout-based rewards.
The evaluation includes several graph-RAG baselines, component and input ablations, a second LLM backbone, cancer-type holdouts, and an external pediatric cancer dataset.
The authors provide useful implementation details and plan to release code and data-processing pipelines.
The generated subgraphs offer a potentially useful interface for examining model hypotheses, and the external-data results suggest some transfer beyond the primary dataset.
weaknesses: The central explainability claim is not established. The graph generator is rewarded mainly by a binary cancer-versus-noncancer classifier, not by CRISPR-target correctness or disease-mechanism fidelity. Because every Target-QA instance is cancerous, this reward can favor generic oncogenic or housekeeping subnetworks rather than cell-line-specific mechanisms.

The reported GNN reward model was selected using test accuracy, constituting test-set model-selection leakage. Its near-perfect cancer-status accuracy on only 336 highly imbalanced samples is also insufficiently investigated, while its edge-prediction AUC is only 0.644.

Target-QA contains just 363 cell lines, yet the primary evaluation uses random 80/20 splits. Closely related cell lines and strongly shared top-100 essential-gene labels can therefore occur across train and test. Cancer-type holdouts help, but lack matched baseline results and do not address unseen laboratories, graph versions, or temporal generalization.

Most performance comes from direct Target-QA supervision: the QA-finetuned LLM already obtains F1 0.5094, versus 0.5399 for GALAX. The incremental gain is modest, no statistical significance testing is provided, and the four-seed uncertainty does not clearly incorporate all stochastic stages or selection among training runs.

Baseline fairness is questionable. RoG, SubgraphRAG, and GNN-RAG are adapted using noisy ChatGPT-generated reasoning paths, whereas GALAX receives bespoke graph supervision and constraints. Multiomics2Targets is used outside its natural cohort-level setting. This makes the claimed superiority over graph-augmented alternatives inconclusive.

The metric definitions are inadequate and potentially inconsistent. The paper requests and labels 100 targets but reports differing precision and recall, and its so-called Hit@5 is frequently higher than Hit@10, contrary to the usual monotonic hit-rate definition. The exact matching, ranking, NER failure handling, and aggregation procedures are not specified.

The biological validation is weak and partly circular: subgraphs start from disease-associated proteins and known KG edges, after which enrichment against related pathway and disease databases is presented as independent support. Human evaluation covers only ten apparently selected examples, supplies evaluators with enrichment results, and lacks blinding, baseline comparisons, agreement analysis, and a selection protocol.

A structurally valid known edge is not necessarily a valid causal signaling step in the given cell line. The rule reward and greedy positive-reward gating therefore do not prevent reward hacking or justify descriptions such as authoritative, mechanistic, or biologically grounded.

The system is evaluated on established cancer cell lines rather than patients, so repeated claims of patient-specific precision medicine are unsupported. No wet-lab validation, perturbational validation of newly proposed targets, safety analysis, or comparison against simple essential-gene and cancer-type frequency baselines is included.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: key graph construction and split details are underspecified, proprietary API models are used for NER and baseline supervision, computational cost is not measured empirically, and several terminology and reporting inconsistencies make the pipeline difficult to reconstruct exactly.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: combining multi-omic measurements, biomedical knowledge graphs, and language models for interpretable cancer-target prioritization.

GALAX is an ambitious integration of an LLM, a graph encoder, and reinforcement-guided subgraph construction. The generated graph provides a more inspectable intermediate representation than an answer-only LLM.
The evaluation includes multiple graph-RAG baselines, component and input ablations, cancer-type holdouts, an external pediatric dataset, and a second LLM backbone.
The authors provide useful implementation details and report results across many cancer cohorts rather than only an aggregate score.
weaknesses: The process reward is poorly aligned with the claimed task. Its principal learned component is a binary cancer-versus-noncancer graph classifier, while every Target-QA instance is a cancer cell line and the downstream task is gene-essentiality ranking. A subgraph that raises generic cancer probability is not necessarily cell-line-specific, target-relevant, causal, or mechanistically correct. KG edge validity likewise establishes only that an interaction is recorded, not that the generated cascade explains a dependency.

There is a serious potential leakage problem. The appendix states that the 363 Target-QA samples overlap with graph-pretraining samples, but it does not demonstrate that test cell lines were excluded from every foundation-model and representation-training stage. The graph classifier checkpoint is also selected using test accuracy. Consequently, the reward model and embeddings may have seen evaluation samples, undermining the claimed generalization.

The main random cell-line split does not control for ubiquitous essential genes or closely related cell lines. Because both predictions and references contain 100 genes, a global target-frequency baseline, cancer-type frequency baseline, nearest-neighbor method, and straightforward supervised multi-omic ranker are essential. Without them, an LLM can obtain substantial overlap by learning common CRISPR dependencies rather than using sample-specific omics or graph reasoning.

The gains over the strongest task-tuned baseline are modest: overall F1 rises from 0.5094 to 0.5399. No paired significance tests or sample-level confidence intervals are provided. GALAX is also not consistently best across individual cohorts, despite overly broad claims of consistent superiority.

Baseline fairness is questionable. RoG, SubgraphRAG, and GNN-RAG are trained using reasoning paths synthesized by ChatGPT 5.1 because native annotations are unavailable; the paper itself characterizes these paths as noisy and incomplete. This may disadvantage the comparison methods and does not isolate the value of GALAX's reinforcement-learning formulation.

The evaluation metrics are insufficiently defined and inconsistently named. Tables call the metrics Hit@5 and Hit@10, whereas an appendix figure calls them precision@5 and precision@10. Reported Hit@5 values can exceed Hit@10, which is incompatible with the conventional hit-rate definition. Macro versus micro aggregation and handling of outputs with fewer or more than 100 recognized genes are also unclear.

The explainability evidence does not establish faithfulness or mechanistic validity. Enrichment is nearly guaranteed to find broad cancer pathways in subgraphs constrained to a biomedical KG and can be circular when source and evaluation databases overlap. Human evaluation covers only ten apparently selected examples, has no competing-method or random-subgraph controls, and gives evaluators enrichment results that may reveal the expected cancer label. Raters judge generic cancer-type correspondence rather than whether edges causally explain the predicted CRISPR targets.

The manuscript repeatedly describes cell-line experiments as patient-specific precision medicine and predicted essential genes as therapeutic targets. DepMap in-vitro knockout effects do not establish patient specificity, druggability, selectivity, safety, or clinical efficacy, so the biomedical conclusions substantially exceed the evidence.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the stated code release: cohort construction and graph-pretraining populations are inconsistent across sections, the stochastic retry and best-subgraph selection procedure is underspecified, several stages depend on external proprietary LLM APIs, and the exact prompts and settings for NER and baseline-path generation are not adequately documented.

Overall, the framework is interesting, but leakage risk, reward-task misalignment, missing trivial yet crucial baselines, ambiguous metrics, and weak explanation validation prevent the central accuracy and mechanistic-interpretability claims from being considered reliable at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem—cell-line-specific CRISPR target prioritization—and presents a coherent integration of multi-omic features, biomedical graphs, language models, and stepwise subgraph generation.
GALAX is technically interesting: a frozen GNN, schema constraints, rollout rewards, and quality gating provide a structured alternative to unconstrained language-model reasoning.

The empirical study is broad, including several graph-RAG baselines, two LLM backbones, component and input ablations, cancer-type holdouts, an external pediatric dataset, and limited expert evaluation.
Aggregate results are consistently favorable: GALAX improves over the strongest reported baselines on Target-QA, and reward-component ablations generally support the full design.
The proposed Target-QA resource and generated subgraphs could be useful to researchers studying graph-language modeling for precision medicine.
weaknesses: The evaluation lacks a crucial global target-frequency or generic-essential-gene baseline. CRISPR dependencies are strongly shared across cell lines, and random cell-line splitting permits a task-tuned LLM to memorize commonly essential genes. The large jump after Target-QA tuning, together with the absence of this baseline, makes it unclear how much performance reflects patient-specific reasoning rather than label-frequency learning.

The reward model is trained to distinguish cancerous from non-cancerous samples, not to assess whether a proposed edge or target is causally relevant to the specific CRISPR outcome. Because every downstream example is cancerous, maximizing this score may favor generic oncogenic subnetworks rather than faithful, cell-line-specific mechanisms.

The mechanistic-interpretability evidence is not yet convincing. Enrichment is performed on subgraphs already constructed from disease-associated and PPI knowledge, making cancer-pathway enrichment partly expected. Human evaluation covers only ten apparently selected examples, supplies evaluators with enrichment results, lacks blinding and inter-rater agreement analysis, and includes no comparison against baseline subgraphs.

Baseline fairness and reproducibility are uncertain: competing retrievers receive GPT-5.1-generated reasoning paths because genuine paths are unavailable, while GALAX uses a different supervision mechanism. Implementation details for this synthetic supervision, graph rules, NER mapping, subgraph selection, and adaptive retry procedure are insufficient to reproduce or audit the comparison.

Reported gains over the strongest baseline are modest and no paired significance tests or confidence intervals for the performance differences are provided. Several cohort-level tables also show baselines outperforming GALAX, despite stronger claims in the text.

Metric definitions are unclear. Quantities called Hit@5 and Hit@10 behave like precision@k—Hit@5 can exceed Hit@10—and are labeled precision@k elsewhere in the appendix. The relationships among extracted output size, precision, recall, and the fixed top-100 reference set need explicit definition.

The dataset is small (363 examples), the main split is random rather than grouped by cancer type or relatedness, and the external dataset uses closely related CRISPR dependency data. The holdout experiment has no competing-model results, so it does not establish that GALAX generalizes better than alternatives.

There are notable methodological inconsistencies, including an advertised 80/20 split that is actually 300/63, conflicting descriptions of random seeds and best-run checkpoint selection, an implausibly described one-dimensional BioBERT text embedding, and incomplete public-resource links. These issues weaken confidence in reproducibility and the strength of the central claims.
